title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning, with a particular focus on prompting literacy. The authors note that while generative AI tools are increasingly available in schools, few interventions teach secondary students when to use AI for learning, how to formulate effective prompts, and how to avoid unproductive or unethical uses such as asking directly for answers. The study also examines whether an AI-based auto-grader can accurately assess student-written prompts and support learning through immediate feedback.

The intervention was a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based prompting practice. Students first reviewed learning objectives and completed conceptual practice, then engaged in three subject-specific scenarios in biology, geography, and math. In each scenario, students wrote prompts to an AI chatbot, viewed the chatbot response, and then received automated rubric-based feedback on dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, background/context, elaboration, and avoiding direct-answer requests where appropriate. The module was grounded in learning-by-doing and immediate elaborated feedback, and used GPT-4o for chatbot interaction and auto-grading.

The intervention was deployed in authentic secondary school classrooms during information technology classes. Study 1 took place in June 2024 across 6 secondary classrooms in East Asia and yielded valid data from 111 students; it combined quantitative analyses of prompt quality, confidence, and pre/post assessments with qualitative thematic analysis of student reflections. Study 2 followed with the same procedure and a similar population in additional classrooms, contributing to a total of 11 authentic secondary classrooms across two iterations. Teachers facilitated the classroom sessions, and students were warned that the auto-grader could make mistakes.

The paper concludes that the AI-based auto-grader achieved generally strong grading performance, with average classification accuracy around 0.92, and that the module helped students improve certain prompting skills, especially including background/context in prompts. Students also reported higher confidence in using AI for learning after the activity. However, multiple-choice assessments showed ceiling effects, leading the authors to revise the assessment in Study 2; analyses suggested that true/false and open-ended items measured prompting literacy better than the original multiple-choice items. Overall, the findings suggest promise for scalable prompting-literacy instruction, while also indicating the need for broader studies, stronger assessment instruments, and further refinement of the grading system.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational large language model used here both as the underlying chatbot and as an AI auto-grader within a web-based prompting literacy instructional module.
identified_tools.use_case: In this paper, GPT-4o powered a K-12 prompting literacy module where secondary students wrote prompts in biology, geography, and math scenarios, received chatbot responses, and then received immediate rubric-based auto-grading and feedback on their prompts.

findings.finding_summary: The GPT-4o-based auto-grader achieved high agreement with human scoring on student-written prompts. Average pass/fail classification accuracy across rubric dimensions was high, including Relevance=0.98, Purpose=0.85, Conciseness=0.93, Background=0.96, Elaboration=0.90, and No Direct Answer=0.88; overall explanation accuracy was 0.95. Study 1 analyzed 483 unique student-written prompts from 111 students.
findings.measure: Auto-grader accuracy against human rubric scoring of student prompts
findings.effect_size: Accuracy values: 0.85-0.98 by dimension; explanation accuracy=0.95

findings.finding_summary: Students improved in including background/context in prompts after using the module supported by GPT-4o feedback. McNemar tests showed the proportion correctly including Background was significantly higher in Q3 than Q1 (p=.039), while no significant differences were found for Relevance (p>.90), Conciseness (p=.286), or Purpose (p=.617).
findings.measure: Human-graded prompt quality across practice tasks by rubric dimension

findings.finding_summary: Students reported greater confidence in using AI for learning after the GPT-4o-based activity. Self-reported confidence increased by 10.4% on average (SD=0.92), and the pre-post Wilcoxon test showed this increase was significant (p<.001).
findings.measure: 5-point Likert self-reported confidence in knowing how to use AI to help learning

findings.finding_summary: There was no significant improvement on the multiple-choice prompting literacy pre/post assessment in Study 1. Among 98 students completing both tests, pre-test performance (Mean=4.4, Median=5.0, SD=1.04, full score=6.0) and post-test performance (Mean=4.4, Median=5.0, SD=0.96) did not differ significantly (p=.377), which the authors attribute to a ceiling effect.

Assessment revisions informed by Study 1 produced better-performing items in Study 2 for measuring prompting literacy within the GPT-4o-supported module. None of the original MCQ items fell in the desired difficulty/discrimination range, whereas 60% of open-ended and 30% of true/false revised items did; reliability was moderate with Cronbach's alpha=0.68 for the original assessment and 0.58 for the iterated version.
findings.measure: Assessment item difficulty, discrimination index, and Cronbach's alpha

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical classroom deployment with mixed methods, pre/post measures, human-vs-AI grading comparison, and assessment analysis, but it does not report a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison group. Findings are promising but primarily from iterative implementation studies.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive changes in confidence and one significant improvement in prompt background inclusion, plus strong auto-grader accuracy, but most learning impacts are reported without standardized effect sizes and one pre/post assessment result was null. Overall impact appears promising but still unclear in magnitude.
